Grammar

Chinese Grammar

Essential grammar patterns and structures for mastering Chinese

Personal Pronouns

Chinese verbs don't conjugate - they stay the same regardless of the subject! Only the pronoun changes.

我
wǒ
I, me
你
nǐ
you (singular)
他/她/它
tā / tā / tā
he / she / it
我们
wǒmen
we, us
你们
nǐmen
you (plural)
他们/她们/它们
tāmen / tāmen / tāmen
they (male/female/things)

Example: 我是 (wǒ shì - I am), 你是 (nǐ shì - you are), 他是 (tā shì - he is) - notice 是 (shì) never changes!

Tense & Time (Past, Present, Future)

Chinese verbs don't change for tense! Instead, use time words and particles to indicate when something happens.

Present / Habitual Actions

我吃饭
wǒ chī fàn
I eat / I am eating

Past Tense (了 le - completed action)

我吃了饭
wǒ chī le fàn
I ate / I have eaten
我昨天去了北京
wǒ zuótiān qù le běijīng
I went to Beijing yesterday

Past Experience (过 guo - have done before)

我去过中国
wǒ qù guo zhōngguó
I have been to China (before)

Future Tense (会 huì / 要 yào - will / going to)

我会去
wǒ huì qù
I will go
我明天要去北京
wǒ míngtiān yào qù běijīng
I'm going to go to Beijing tomorrow

Modal Verbs (Should, Would, Can, Must)

Modal verbs are placed before the main verb and never change form.

Should / Ought to (应该 yīnggāi)

你应该学习
nǐ yīnggāi xuéxí
You should study
我们应该去
wǒmen yīnggāi qù
We should go

Would like (想 xiǎng / 想要 xiǎng yào)

我想吃饭
wǒ xiǎng chī fàn
I would like to eat / I want to eat
你想去吗？
nǐ xiǎng qù ma?
Would you like to go?

Can / Be able to (能 néng / 可以 kěyǐ / 会 huì)

我会说中文
wǒ huì shuō zhōngwén
I can speak Chinese (learned skill)
我可以帮你
wǒ kěyǐ bāng nǐ
I can help you (permission/possibility)
我能做
wǒ néng zuò
I can do it (physical ability)

Must / Have to (必须 bìxū / 得 děi)

我必须去
wǒ bìxū qù
I must go
你得学习
nǐ děi xuéxí
You have to study

Do / Did (emphasis - use 是...的 structure)

我是昨天去的
wǒ shì zuótiān qù de
I DID go yesterday (emphasis on when)
他是开车来的
tā shì kāichē lái de
He DID come by car (emphasis on how)

Word Order (SVO)

Chinese follows Subject-Verb-Object order, similar to English.

我 吃 饭
wǒ chī fàn
I eat rice (I-eat-rice)

的 (de) - Possessive

Used to show possession or to modify nouns (like 's or "of" in English).

我的书
wǒ de shū
my book
他的朋友
tā de péngyou
his/her friend

了 (le) - Completed Action

Indicates a completed action or change of state.

我吃了饭
wǒ chī le fàn
I ate (have eaten) rice
他去了中国
tā qù le zhōngguó
He went to China

吗 (ma) - Yes/No Questions

Add 吗 (ma) at the end of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question.

你吃饭吗？
nǐ chī fàn ma?
Do you eat rice?
他是学生吗？
tā shì xuésheng ma?
Is he a student?

不 (bù) / 没 (méi) - Negation

不 (bù) negates present/future actions. 没 (méi) negates past actions or possession.

我不吃肉
wǒ bù chī ròu
I don't eat meat
我没吃饭
wǒ méi chī fàn
I didn't eat / haven't eaten

在 (zài) - Location

Indicates location or ongoing action (similar to "at" or "-ing").

我在家
wǒ zài jiā
I'm at home
他在学习
tā zài xuéxí
He is studying

Measure Words

Used between numbers and nouns. Different nouns require different measure words.

一个人 (general)
yī gè rén
one person
一本书 (books)
yī běn shū
one book
一杯茶 (cups)
yī bēi chá
one cup of tea

比 (bǐ) - Comparison

Used to make comparisons between two things (A 比 B + adjective).

我比你高
wǒ bǐ nǐ gāo
I am taller than you
今天比昨天冷
jīntiān bǐ zuótiān lěng
Today is colder than yesterday

Time-Manner-Place

In Chinese, time comes first, then manner, then place (unlike English).

我明天早上在学校学习
wǒ míngtiān zǎoshang zài xuéxiào xuéxí
I will study at school tomorrow morning

Essential measure words (classifiers) used between numbers and nouns in Chinese

How to Use Measure Words

Structure: Number + Measure Word + Noun

一个人
yī gè rén
one person
三本书
sān běn shū
three books
两杯茶
liǎng bēi chá
two cups of tea

Tip: When in doubt, 个 (gè) is the most common and versatile measure word!

How to Tell Time in Chinese

Basic Structure: Hour + 点 (diǎn) + Minutes + 分 (fēn)

  • On the hour: 三点 (sān diǎn) = 3:00
  • With minutes: 三点二十分 (sān diǎn èrshí fēn) = 3:20
  • Half past: 三点半 (sān diǎn bàn) = 3:30
  • Quarter hours: 三点一刻 (sān diǎn yī kè) = 3:15
  • Minutes to the hour: 差五分四点 (chà wǔ fēn sì diǎn) = 3:55 (5 minutes to 4)
  • Note: Use 两 (liǎng) instead of 二 (èr) for 2 o'clock: 两点 (liǎng diǎn)

Chinese History & Culture

Explore the rich tapestry of Chinese civilization spanning over 5,000 years

Major Chinese Dynasties (朝代 - Cháodài)

Chinese history is traditionally divided into dynastic periods, each leaving unique cultural and technological legacies.

Semi-legendary first dynasty, foundation of Chinese civilization

Legendary Figures & Philosophers

Individuals who shaped Chinese thought, culture, and governance throughout history.

Philosophers & Thinkers

Confucius (孔子 - Kǒngzǐ) 551-479 BCE

Founder of Confucianism, emphasizing morality, family loyalty, and respect for elders. His teachings became the foundation of Chinese society and governance for millennia. Famous quote: "Learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is perilous."

Laozi (老子 - Lǎozǐ) 6th century BCE

Legendary founder of Taoism (道教 - Dàojiào) and author of the Tao Te Ching (道德经 - Dàodéjīng). Advocated living in harmony with the Tao (道 - "the Way"), emphasizing simplicity, spontaneity, and non-action (无为 - wúwéi).

Mencius (孟子 - Mèngzǐ) 372-289 BCE

Second most important Confucian philosopher. Believed in the inherent goodness of human nature and the right of people to overthrow unjust rulers. His ideas influenced Chinese political philosophy.

Sun Tzu (孙子 - Sūnzǐ) 544-496 BCE

Military strategist and author of The Art of War (孙子兵法 - Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ), one of history's most influential military treatises. His principles extend beyond warfare into business and life strategy.

Emperors & Leaders

Qin Shi Huang (秦始皇 - Qín Shǐhuáng) 259-210 BCE

First Emperor of unified China (Qin Dynasty). Standardized writing, currency, and measurements. Initiated Great Wall construction and built the famous Terracotta Army. His reign was both transformative and authoritarian.

Emperor Wu of Han (汉武帝 - Hàn Wǔdì) 156-87 BCE

Expanded Han Dynasty territory, established Confucianism as state ideology, and opened the Silk Road for trade with the West. His 54-year reign marked a golden age of Chinese power and culture.

Empress Wu Zetian (武则天 - Wǔ Zétiān) 624-705 CE

The only female emperor in Chinese history. Rose from concubine to empress to emperor during Tang Dynasty. Known for promoting capable officials based on merit and expanding the empire's influence.

Kublai Khan (忽必烈 - Hūbìliè) 1215-1294 CE

Mongol grandson of Genghis Khan who founded the Yuan Dynasty. Completed the conquest of China and promoted cultural exchange between East and West. Hosted Marco Polo at his court.

Poets & Artists

Li Bai (李白 - Lǐ Bái) 701-762 CE

One of China's greatest poets from Tang Dynasty, known as the "Immortal Poet." His romantic, imaginative verses celebrated nature, friendship, and wine. Wrote over 1,000 poems, many memorized by Chinese students today.

Du Fu (杜甫 - Dù Fǔ) 712-770 CE

Another Tang Dynasty master, known as the "Poet Sage." His realistic, socially conscious poetry depicted the suffering of ordinary people during times of war and hardship. His technical skill was unmatched.

The Silk Road (丝绸之路 - Sīchóu Zhī Lù)

Ancient network of trade routes connecting China with the Mediterranean, Central Asia, and Europe. Facilitated exchange of goods (silk, spices, tea), technologies, religions (Buddhism spread to China), and ideas for over 1,500 years. Named for Chinese silk, the most sought-after commodity.

Click for details

The Great Wall (长城 - Chángchéng)

One of humanity's most impressive architectural achievements. While walls existed earlier, Qin Shi Huang connected and extended them around 221 BCE. The Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) built most of the wall visible today. Stretches over 13,000 miles, built to protect against northern invasions.

Click for details

Zheng He's Voyages (郑和下西洋 - Zhèng Hé Xià Xīyáng)

Between 1405-1433, Admiral Zheng He led seven massive naval expeditions during Ming Dynasty. His fleet of "treasure ships" reached Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa—decades before European explorers. Demonstrated China's maritime power and promoted trade and diplomacy.

Click for details

Imperial Examination System (科举 - Kējǔ)

Established during Sui Dynasty (581-618 CE) and perfected under Tang. This merit-based civil service exam system selected government officials based on knowledge of Confucian classics rather than birth or connections. Influenced East Asian education for over 1,300 years and inspired modern civil service systems worldwide.

Click for details

Cultural Concepts & Philosophy

Filial Piety (孝 - Xiào)

Central Confucian virtue emphasizing respect, obedience, and care for one's parents and ancestors. Considered the foundation of moral character and social harmony in traditional Chinese culture.

Yin and Yang (阴阳 - Yīnyáng)

Ancient concept describing complementary opposites—dark/light, female/male, passive/active. Rather than conflict, they create balance and harmony. Fundamental to Chinese philosophy, medicine, and martial arts.

Five Elements (五行 - Wǔxíng)

Wood (木 - mù), Fire (火 - huǒ), Earth (土 - tǔ), Metal (金 - jīn), and Water (水 - shuǐ). These elements interact in cycles of creation and destruction, used to explain natural phenomena, medicine, feng shui, and even political theory.

The Mandate of Heaven (天命 - Tiānmìng)

Zhou Dynasty concept stating that heaven grants emperors the right to rule based on their virtue. If a ruler became corrupt or ineffective, heaven would withdraw the mandate, justifying rebellion and the rise of a new dynasty. This cyclical view shaped Chinese political philosophy.

Cultural Learning Tip

Understanding Chinese history and culture deepens your language learning. Many Chinese idioms (成语 - chéngyǔ), expressions, and even characters have historical origins. For example, "三顾茅庐" (sān gù máo lú - "three visits to a thatched cottage") refers to a famous story from the Three Kingdoms period, now meaning persistent effort to recruit talented people.

Geography Learning Tip

Many Chinese province and city names have meaningful characters! For example, 北京 (Běijīng) means "Northern Capital" (北 = north, 京 = capital), while 南京 (Nánjīng) means "Southern Capital." Understanding these characters helps you remember locations and learn vocabulary at the same time!
